[notes-n1] Notes 1. Columns on the site boundary
A column on the site boundary cannot stand at the centre of a pad: the pad would have to cross the boundary into the neighbour’s land. Built flush with the boundary, the pad takes the column load at one edge, and Unit 10’s rule gives the result: the pressure becomes a short, very high triangle and the pad rotates.
[Figure: Column A of Worked Example 11.1 on its pad alone, and with the strap. Alone: e = 0.85 m is beyond L/3, contact over 0.45 m, 1365 kN/m² (the weight of the pad left out).]
With the numbers of Worked Example 11.1: column A carries 1075 kN (service) and stands 0.15 m from the boundary on a pad 2.0 m long and 3.5 m wide. Then e = 1.0 − 0.15 = 0.85 m, beyond L/6 = 0.33 m and even beyond L/3 = 0.67 m, where EC7 6.5.4 asks for special precautions. The contact length is L_c = 3(1.0 − 0.85) = 0.45 m and p_{max} = 2 × 1075/(3.5 × 0.45) = 1365 kN/m², almost seven times an allowable 200 kN/m². The pad would settle at the boundary and tilt the column.
[Figure: Three ways out: a rectangular combined footing, a trapezoidal combined footing, or a strap footing.]
Foundation Use it when Pressure
Rectangular combined footing (Unit 10) Column B is close, and the base can run past it far enough for its centroid to sit on the resultant: L = 2 × (distance from the boundary to the resultant). uniform
Trapezoidal combined footing (§4) The length is fixed at both ends (a second boundary, a lift pit, a drain), so a rectangle cannot put its centroid on the resultant. The wide end goes to the heavier column. uniform, or nearly
Strap footing (§2, §3) The columns are far apart, so a combined footing would be long and heavy. Each column keeps its own footing, and a strap beam ties them so that footing A stays level. uniform under each footing
The strap is what EC2 calls a tie beam (9.8.3): a beam that removes the eccentricity of the loading of the foundations, designed for the bending moments and shear forces that result. It must not bear on the soil, so the ground under it is loosened and left uncompacted (Mosley §10.3). Where compaction machinery can act on it, EC2 asks for a downward load of q_1 = 10 kN/m as well.
Quick check (not graded): A boundary column and an inner column 6.5 m apart both carry about 1500 kN. The ground is good near the surface. Which foundation is the usual choice for the boundary column?
Options: A pad under column A alone, flush with the boundary | A rectangular combined footing about 13 m long | A strap footing | A raft
Explanation shown after answering: Far-apart columns call for a strap footing: each keeps its own footing and the strap keeps footing A level. A rectangular combined footing centred on the resultant would run about twice the distance from the boundary to the resultant, more than 13 m; the pad alone would rotate.
Key points:
- A pad flush with the boundary takes its column at one edge: e is far beyond L/6, and the pad rotates.
- Three ways out: a rectangular combined footing, a trapezoidal one, or a strap footing; far-apart columns take the strap.
- The strap is a tie beam (EC2 9.8.3): designed for its moment and shear, and kept off the soil.

[notes-n2] Notes 2. The strap footing: statics
The strap and its two footings act as one rigid body. Take moments about column B: column A’s load, standing at the boundary, tries to tip the strap about the centre of footing A, and column B’s load holds the far end down. Like a seesaw, the reaction under footing A comes out larger than column A’s own load.
[Figure: The strap as a lever. Without the weights, R_A = N_AL/(L − e) and R_B = N_B − N_Ae/(L − e).]
Let L be the distance between the column centres, L_A the length of footing A along the strap (it starts at the boundary) and c_A the width of column A. Column A stands c_A/2 from the boundary and the centre of footing A is L_A/2 from it, so the lever arm is e = L_A/2 − c_A/2. With the weights of the footings W_A, W_B and of the strap W_R (centroid x_R from column B), moments about column B and the vertical forces give Mosley’s Eqs. 10.5 and 10.6:
EQUATION (11.1): R_A = W_A + \frac{N_A\,L + W_R\,x_R}{L - e}, \qquad e = \frac{L_A}{2} - \frac{c_A}{2}
EQUATION (11.2): R_B = N_A + N_B + W_A + W_B + W_R - R_A
EQUATION (11.3): B_A = \frac{R_A}{q_{all}\,L_A}, \qquad S_B = \sqrt{\frac{R_B}{q_{all}}}
The course method for a strap footing Size, with the service loads. Take the footing weights first as 10 % of the column loads and the strap weight between the column faces; choose L_A; find R_A by Eq. (11.1), the width B_A, then R_B and the side S_B of a square footing B by Eqs. (11.2) and (11.3), rounded up. Then put in the actual weights and check both pressures; widen a footing if a pressure exceeds q_{all}. Design, with the ultimate loads. Repeat Eq. (11.1) with N_{Ed} and 1.35W_R but without the footing weights, which bear straight on the soil and cause no moment: R_{A,Ed} = (N_{A,Ed}L + 1.35W_Rx_R)/(L − e), R_{B,Ed} = N_{A,Ed} + N_{B,Ed} + 1.35W_R − R_{A,Ed}, and each footing its own pressure p_A = R_{A,Ed}/(L_AB_A), p_B = R_{B,Ed}/S_B².
EQUATION (11.4): R_{A,Ed} = \frac{N_{A,Ed}\,L + 1.35\,W_R\,x_R}{L - e}, \qquad p_A = \frac{R_{A,Ed}}{L_A B_A}, \quad p_B = \frac{R_{B,Ed}}{S_B^{\,2}}
Step (Worked Example 11.1) Calculation Output

Footing A B_A = 1382.3/(200 × 2.0) = 3.46 3.5 m
Footing B R_B = 1075 + 1725 + 107.5 + 172.5 + 38.5 − 1382.3 = 1736.1; S_B = √(1736.1/200) 2.95 m

Two things follow from Eq. (11.1). A longer footing A moves its centre away from the column, so e grows and R_A grows with it, while footing A gets narrower. A column B closer to A shortens L − e and also raises R_A. Column B pays for the lever: R_B = N_B − N_Ae/(L − e). If column B is light, R_B could fall towards zero and the strap would lift it, so R_B must stay well positive with the smallest load column B can carry.
Mosley takes one pressure for both footings at the ultimate limit state when the dead-to-imposed load ratios of the two columns are similar. The course method keeps the pressure of each footing from statics: in Worked Example 11.1, 252.7 and 254.3 kN/m² against one value of 253.6 kN/m². The difference is small, but statics closes the moment diagram exactly, and one pressure does not (Notes §3).
Quick check (not graded): Leave out the weights. Column A carries 800 kN; the column centres are 5.0 m apart; footing A is 1.8 m long and column A is 0.3 m wide. R_A is
Options: 800 kN | 941 kN | 686 kN | 1067 kN
Explanation shown after answering: e = 0.9 − 0.15 = 0.75 m; R_A = 800 × 5.0/(5.0 − 0.75) = 941 kN, 18 % more than the column load. Column B gives up the same 141 kN.
Key points:
- Moments about column B: R_A = W_A + (N_AL + W_Rx_R)/(L − e), e = L_A/2 − c_A/2; R_B from the vertical forces.
- R_A > N_A and R_B < N_B: the strap carries N_Ae to column B.
- Size with service loads (10 % weights, then the actual ones); design with net ultimate reactions, each footing its own pressure.

[notes-n3] Notes 3. Designing a strap footing
Three members come out of the statics: the strap beam, footing A and footing B. The strap is loaded by the columns at their centres, pushed up by each footing over its length, and pulled down by its own weight between the column faces. Its shear force and bending moment follow as for any beam, and they decide where its bars and links go.
[Figure: Strap of Worked Example 11.1: loads, shear force and bending moment (drawn on the tension side).]
Over footing A the upward pressure w_A = p_AB_A works against column A: the shear is largest at the face of column A and falls to zero at x_0 from the boundary, where the moment is largest and hogging (top in tension). Between the footings the shear is nearly constant and the moment falls in a straight line. Round column B the moment changes sign: that is footing B bending as a pad under its own column, designed with footing B.
EQUATION (11.5): x_0 = \frac{N_{A,Ed} - w_r\,c_A}{w_A - w_r}, \qquad M_{max} = w_A\frac{x_0^{\,2}}{2} - N_{A,Ed}\left(x_0 - \frac{c_A}{2}\right) - w_r\frac{(x_0 - c_A)^2}{2}
The strap beam (audit D28, D35) Bars. The main bars go at the top, for M_{max}; d comes from the actual bar layers (5H32 fit three to a layer in a 300 mm strap, so d = 810 mm). Worked Example 11.1 gives K = 0.177 > 0.167, so it needs compression bars: A_{s2} = 174 mm² (2H16 at the bottom) and A_s = 3586 mm² (5H32). Bottom bars are wanted anyway, for differential settlement and downward loads (Mosley §10.3). Links. The largest shear is over footing A, near column A: 517.7 kN at d from its face, against 261 kN between the footings. With θ = 22°, A_{sw}/s = V_{Ed}/(0.78f_{yk}d cot θ) = 0.662 mm²/mm, so H8 at 150 mm (0.670) over footing A and H6 at 150 mm (0.377 ≥ 0.334) elsewhere. Foundation3.xlsx checked the shear between the footings only.
Footing A: one-way, from the strap The strap carries footing A along its length, so footing A spans across the strap only, as two cantilevers from the faces of the strap: l_A = (B_A − b_s)/2 = (3.5 − 0.3)/2 = 1.6 m and M_A = p_AL_Al_A²/2 = 252.7 × 2.0 × 1.6²/2 = 647.0 kN m. The main bars run across, in the outer layer (d = 652 mm): 12H16. Shear at d from the strap face: 479.2 ≤ 484.2 kN, with the bars too short to count. Column A has no punching perimeter in footing A: it stands on the strap, which carries its load.
EQUATION (11.6): M_A = p_A\,L_A\,\frac{l_A^{\,2}}{2}, \qquad l_A = \frac{B_A - b_s}{2}
Footing B is an ordinary pad under column B (Unit 10): the moment at the column face each way, 658.5 kN m, gives 15H16 each way with the minimum steel governing; shear at d passes (516.8 ≤ 701.3 kN). For punching, the strap carries its own shear into column B, so the force on a perimeter is the soil pressure outside it, V_{Ed,red} = p_B(S_B² − A(a)): 0.08 against 0.37 N/mm² at 2d, and 0.69 at the worst perimeter inside 2d (a = 0.75d).
Quick check (not graded): How does footing A of a strap footing bend?
Options: In both directions, like a pad round column A | Across the strap only, as two cantilevers from the strap faces | Along the strap only | It does not bend: the strap carries everything
Explanation shown after answering: The strap supports footing A along its length, so footing A spans across: two cantilevers of l_A = (B_A − b_s)/2 from the strap faces, with its main bars across. Along the strap the strap itself does the work.
Key points:
- The strap hogs over footing A and between the footings: main bars at the top, largest moment at zero shear (Eq. 11.5).
- The largest strap shear is over footing A, near column A: heavy links there, lighter ones between the footings.
- Footing A: one-way cantilevers from the strap faces. Footing B: a pad, with punching from the soil pressure outside each perimeter.

[notes-n4] Notes 4. The trapezoidal combined footing
A combined footing works by putting the centroid of its plan on the resultant of the column loads, so that the pressure is uniform. A rectangle has its centroid at mid-length. When the length is fixed at both ends and the resultant is not at mid-length, a trapezoid moves the centroid towards its wide end, which goes under the heavier column.
EQUATION (11.7): A = \frac{L}{2}\,(b_1 + b_2), \qquad \bar{x} = \frac{L}{3}\cdot\frac{b_1 + 2b_2}{b_1 + b_2}
Here b_1 is the width at the boundary end and x̄ is measured from it. Choose the area A for the service loads, set x̄ on the resultant, and solve the two equations for b_1 and b_2. Case F8 (Foundation3.xlsx Ex 11.5) carries the two columns of Worked Example 11.1 on one base 7.2 m long: the resultant of the service loads lies 3.70 m from column A, so x̄ = 3.85 m from the boundary, past mid-length. With A = 18 m², b_1 + b_2 = 2A/L = 5.0 m and b_1 + 2b_2 = 3x̄(b_1 + b_2)/L = 8.01 m, so b_2 = 3.01 m and b_1 = 1.99 m, rounded to 3.0 and 2.0 m. The service pressure is (2800 + 562.5)/18 = 186.8 ≤ 200 kN/m².
[Figure: Case F8: the trapezoid, its pressure and its bending moment.]
The rounded widths put the ultimate resultant 31 mm off the centroid, so the pressure is linear, 212.2 to 223.7 kN/m² (Foundation3.xlsx kept it uniform). The upward load q(x) = p(x)b(x) is then a quadratic in x, and the course method integrates it exactly for V and M: zero shear at 3.13 m and a hogging moment of 2200 kN m, top bars 24H16. The spreadsheet’s triangle approximation gave 2099 kN m, 4.6 % low. At the ultimate limit state the vertical shear governs at d from the inner face of column A (818.0 ≤ 850.2 kN, with the narrower width there), and punching passes at both columns (0.59 at A, 0.43 at B).
Quick check (not graded): Why is footing F8 wider at the far end than at the boundary?
Options: To reduce the moment between the columns | Because column A is the heavier one | Column B carries more, so the resultant lies past mid-length; the wide end pulls the centroid onto it | To keep the strap short
Explanation shown after answering: Column B carries 1725 kN against 1075 kN at A, so the resultant of the service loads sits 3.85 m from the boundary, beyond the mid-length of 3.6 m. A trapezoid wide at B puts its centroid there; a rectangle 7.2 m long could not.
Key points:
- Trapezoid: A = L(b_1 + b_2)/2 and x̄ = (L/3)(b_1 + 2b_2)/(b_1 + b_2) on the resultant.
- The wide end goes under the heavier column; use it when the length is fixed at both ends.
- Like any combined footing it hogs between the columns: top bars there.

[notes-n5] Notes 5. Piles: when, which and how many
Piles are used where the soil near the surface is too weak or too compressible for spread footings, or where a firm stratum lies deeper than about 3 m. They extend down to firm soil and carry the load by end bearing, by friction along the shaft, or by both (course notes; Mosley §10.6).
[Figure: End bearing, friction, and the bulb of pressure under a single pile and under a group.]
Requirement What the course uses Source
Type Precast reinforced or prestressed (spun) concrete, driven; cast-in-situ bored piles; timber, steel and bakau piles for lighter work. The choice depends on the loads, the structure, the soil strata and the site. course notes
Capacity A working (service) load per pile, from load tests or a driving formula, the ultimate load divided by a factor of safety of 2 to 3; given by the geotechnical engineer or the pile supplier: 600 kN for a 300 mm square precast pile and 1800 kN for a 500 mm spun pile in the notes’ examples. course notes; Mosley §10.6
Number n = (N + W)/F_p with the service load and an assumed cap weight, rounded up to a symmetrical group (Eq. 11.8). course notes
Spacing s = 3φ_p centre to centre. Mosley’s minimum: the pile perimeter for friction piles, twice the least width for end-bearing piles; for a square friction pile the perimeter, 4b, exceeds 3b. course notes; Mosley §10.6
Cap 150 mm beyond the faces of the outer piles (Eq. 11.9); depth from Mosley Table 10.5 for up to six piles, enough to anchor the column starter bars and the pile bars. Mosley §10.7; course notes
Bored piles Longitudinal steel at least 0.5 % of A_c up to 0.5 m² (25 cm² up to 1.0 m², 0.25 % above), at least six bars of 16 mm or more, clear spacing round the perimeter not over 200 mm. EC2 9.8.5, Table 9.6N
EQUATION (11.8): n = \frac{N + W}{F_p}\ \ \text{(rounded up)}
EQUATION (11.9): s = k\,\phi_p\ \ (k = 3), \qquad B = \left(k\,(n_y - 1) + 1\right)\phi_p + 300
[Figure: Spacing, edge distance and depth of a pile cap, and the common groups.]
The load a group can carry is not always n times the load of one pile. Closely spaced friction piles share the same soil, and a large group can carry about a third less; end-bearing piles on rock or dense gravel carry nearly the full sum. The stressed zone under a group also reaches deeper, so its settlement depends on deeper soil (Mosley §10.6). Piles are rarely driven exactly where drawn, which the design and detailing of the cap must allow for (Mosley §10.7).
Quick check (not graded): A column brings 2400 kN (service) onto piles with a working load of 700 kN each. The cap is assumed to weigh 150 kN. How many piles?
Options: 3 | 3.6 | 4 | 6
Explanation shown after answering: n = (2400 + 150)/700 = 3.64, rounded up to 4, a square group. The capacity is a working load, so the service load goes into the sum, not 1.35G_k + 1.5Q_k.
Key points:
- Piles for weak or compressible ground near the surface, or firm ground deeper than about 3 m; end bearing, friction, or both.
- The pile capacity is a working load: n = (N + W)/F_p with service loads, rounded up to a symmetrical group.
- Spacing 3φ_p; the cap 150 mm past the outer piles; depth from Mosley Table 10.5; a group of friction piles carries less than n single piles.

[notes-n6] Notes 6. Pile loads under a moment
A pile cap is stiff. Under a moment it turns about the centroid of the pile group, so the load in each pile changes in proportion to its distance from that centroid, the same idea as the pressure under an eccentric pad. Piles on the axis of the moment add nothing to it.
EQUATION (11.10): P_i = \frac{N + W}{n} \pm \frac{M_y\,x_i}{\sum x^2} \pm \frac{M_x\,y_i}{\sum y^2}
Here x_i and y_i are the distances of pile i from the centroidal axes of the group and the sums run over every pile (Mosley §10.6; course notes). For a group symmetrical about both axes that is all; Mosley gives the general form for a group that is not. The largest service load must not exceed the working load F_p, and the smallest must stay positive unless the piles are designed for tension.
[Figure: Pile loads under a moment: P = N/n ± Mx/Σx².]
Two load levels again. The check against F_p uses the service loads, with the weight of the cap. The design of the cap in Unit 12 uses the ultimate pile loads, N_{Ed}/n ± M_{Ed}x/Σx², without the cap weight: like the weight of a footing, it goes straight down into the piles and does not bend the cap. Faded Example 11.2 does both for the six piles of the course notes’ Example 5: 531.4 ≤ 600 kN in service and 720.8 kN at the ultimate limit state.
The way the group is turned matters. A 2 × 3 group with the moment along its rows of three has Σx² = 4 × 0.9² = 3.24 m² and an outer pile 0.9 m out; turned through 90°, the same moment acts along rows of two, with Σx² = 6 × 0.45² = 1.215 m² and the outer piles 0.45 m out. The ratio x/Σx² rises from 0.28 to 0.37 m⁻¹, so the outer piles carry more, although their lever arm is half. Horizontal loads larger than the passive resistance of the soil need raking piles (Mosley §10.6).
Quick check (not graded): Nine piles in a 3 × 3 group at 1.2 m centres carry N + W = 4500 kN (service) and a moment of 270 kN m about one axis. The largest pile load is
Options: 537.5 kN | 590 kN | 500 kN | 612.5 kN
Explanation shown after answering: Σx² = 6 × 1.2² = 8.64 m² (the middle row adds nothing); P = 4500/9 + 270 × 1.2/8.64 = 500 + 37.5 = 537.5 kN. Taking Σx² over one row only, 2 × 1.2² = 2.88 m², would give 612.5 kN.
Key points:
- P = (N + W)/n ± M x/Σx² (± the second moment): the cap turns about the centroid of the group.
- Service loads against F_p, none in tension; ultimate loads without the cap weight for the cap design (Unit 12).
- Σx² runs over every pile; turning a group changes Σx² and the largest pile load.

[examples-x3] Example 3 · Explain-type questions
Exam type short written answers Time ≈ 3 min each
Questions
- Why does footing A of a strap footing carry more than column A, and footing B less than column B?
- Why must the strap not bear on the soil?
- Why does the strap need its main bars at the top and its heaviest links over footing A?
- Why is the pile capacity compared with service loads, and why can a group of friction piles carry less than n single piles?
Write your four answers first, then open the model answers one by one.
## Answer 1 The lever
Column A stands at the boundary, e = 0.85 m from the centre of footing A. Moments about column B give R_A(L − e) = N_AL, so R_A = N_AL/(L − e): 1252 kN for N_A = 1075 kN, leaving the weights out. The extra 177 kN, N_Ae/(L − e), comes off column B: R_B = N_B − 177 kN. The two 177 kN forces, 5.15 m apart, make the couple that balances N_Ae, the moment of the eccentric column.
## Answer 2 A strap that bears takes load
The statics assume that all the soil reaction comes up through the two footings. A strap resting on the soil would be pushed up between the footings: the reactions would change, the strap moments with them, and the strap would settle with the soil it rests on. So the ground under it is loosened and left uncompacted (Mosley §10.3), and where compaction machinery can act on the strap EC2 9.8.3 asks for a downward load of 10 kN/m as well.
## Answer 3 Hogging, and a shear peak
Column A pushes the strap down at its end and footing A pushes it up just inside, so the strap hogs from column A to near column B: the tension is at the top. The shear is the soil reaction on footing A coming back to column A, so it is largest at the face of A (1227 kN; 518 kN at d), while between the footings only N_Ae/(L − e) and the weight are left (261 kN). The links follow the shear: H8 @ 150 over footing A, H6 @ 150 beyond.
## Answer 4 A working load, and shared soil
A pile’s capacity is a safe working load: its ultimate geotechnical resistance divided by a factor of 2 to 3, the same idea as q_{all}. So it is compared with the service loads, (N + W)/n ± Mx/Σx², not with 1.35G_k + 1.5Q_k. In a group of friction piles the shafts load the same soil and their stressed zones overlap: a large, closely spaced group can carry about a third less than n single piles, and it settles more because its bulb of pressure reaches deeper (Mosley §10.6). End-bearing piles on rock carry nearly the full sum.

[glossary-allowable-bearing-pressure-q-all] Glossary: allowable bearing pressure q_{all}
allowable bearing pressure q_{all}: The pressure the soil may carry under service loads, set by the geotechnical engineer with a factor of safety against bearing failure and a limit on settlement; both footings of a strap footing are sized against it.

[glossary-bakau-pile] Glossary: bakau pile
bakau pile: A mangrove timber pile, used in Malaysia for light buildings on soft ground; it lasts only where it stays below the water table.

[glossary-blinding] Glossary: blinding
blinding: A thin layer of lean concrete on the excavated ground so that a footing can be cast clean and level; on blinding c_{nom} ≥ 40 mm (EC2 4.4.1.3(4)).

[glossary-bored-pile] Glossary: bored pile
bored pile: A pile cast in a hole drilled in the ground (cast in situ); EC2 9.8.5 and Table 9.6N set its minimum longitudinal steel.

[glossary-boundary-column] Glossary: boundary column
boundary column: A column on the edge of the site: its footing may not project beyond the line, so a pad under it alone would carry the load far off-centre.

[glossary-bulb-of-pressure] Glossary: bulb of pressure
bulb of pressure: The zone of soil stressed by a foundation. A pile group’s bulb reaches deeper than a single pile’s, so the group settles more (Mosley Figure 10.17).

[glossary-eccentricity-of-footing-a-e] Glossary: eccentricity of footing A, e
eccentricity of footing A, e: The distance from column A to the centre of footing A: e = L_A /2 − c_A /2 for a column on the boundary.

[glossary-end-bearing-pile] Glossary: end-bearing pile
end-bearing pile: A pile that carries its load mainly on its toe, on rock or dense soil; a group of them carries nearly n times one pile.

[glossary-friction-pile] Glossary: friction pile
friction pile: A pile that carries its load mainly by skin friction along its shaft. A large, close group can carry about a third less than n single piles (Mosley §10.6).

[glossary-lever-of-the-strap-l-e] Glossary: lever of the strap, L − e
lever of the strap, L − e: The distance from column B to the centre of footing A. Moments about column B give R_A = N_A L/(L − e) without the weights: more than N_A .

[glossary-net-design-reaction] Glossary: net design reaction
net design reaction: The ultimate reaction of a footing without its own weight (R_{A,Ed} , R_{B,Ed} ); the strap weight stays in, at 1.35W_R . It designs the bars.

[glossary-pile-cap] Glossary: pile cap
pile cap: The block that spreads a column load to its piles; sized from the spacing, its edge 150 mm beyond the pile faces in the course rule; designed in Unit 12.

[glossary-pile-foundation] Glossary: pile foundation
pile foundation: Piles carry the load through weak soil down to firm ground, by end bearing, friction or both; used where a spread footing would be uneconomical or impossible.

[glossary-pile-spacing] Glossary: pile spacing
pile spacing: Centre to centre; the course uses 3φ. Mosley §10.6: not less than the pile perimeter for friction piles, and twice the least width for end-bearing piles.

[glossary-precast-pile] Glossary: precast pile
precast pile: A pile made in a yard and driven; it is designed for lifting and stacking as well as for its load, and its head for the hammer (Mosley §10.6).

[glossary-punching-shear] Glossary: punching shear
punching shear: Failure of a footing round a column on a truncated cone; footing B of a strap footing is checked like a pad, at every perimeter up to 2d (EC2 6.4.4(2)).

[glossary-safe-working-load-of-a-pile-f-p] Glossary: safe (working) load of a pile, F_p
safe (working) load of a pile, F_p: The ultimate resistance of a pile divided by a factor of 2 to 3, from a load test or a driving formula; it is compared with service loads.

[glossary-service-and-ultimate-loads] Glossary: service and ultimate loads
service and ultimate loads: G_k + Q_k for the soil and the piles (against q_{all} and F_p ); 1.35G_k + 1.5Q_k for the concrete.

[glossary-strap-beam] Glossary: strap beam
strap beam: The beam that ties a boundary footing to an inner footing. It hogs, so its main bars are at the top, and it must not bear on the soil.

[glossary-strap-footing] Glossary: strap footing
strap footing: A boundary footing tied by a strap beam to an inner footing, so that the pair resists the overturning of the eccentric column (Mosley §10.3).

[glossary-x-of-a-pile-group] Glossary: Σx² of a pile group
Σx² of a pile group: The sum of x² over every pile, x measured from the centroid of the group; it plays the part of the section modulus in P = (N + W)/n ± Mx/Σx².

[glossary-tension-pile] Glossary: tension pile
tension pile: A pile whose load comes out negative under a large moment: it pulls on the cap and must be designed and anchored for tension. The layout is usually changed instead.

[glossary-tie-beam] Glossary: tie beam
tie beam: A beam between footings or pile caps that holds them together or takes an eccentricity; bars at least 8 mm, and a downward load of 10 kN/m where compaction machinery can act on it (EC2 9.8.3).

[glossary-trapezoidal-combined-footing] Glossary: trapezoidal combined footing
trapezoidal combined footing: A combined footing whose length is fixed at both ends: making it wider at the heavier column moves its centroid under the resultant, x̄ = (L/3)(b_1 + 2b_2 )/(b_1 + b_2 ).

[glossary-zero-shear-x-0] Glossary: zero shear x_0
zero shear x_0: The section of the strap where V = 0, over footing A, measured from the boundary; the largest (hogging) moment of the strap is there.
